prompt:
Let $G$ be a group and let $K\subseteq H$ be subgroups of $G$ with $K\trianglelefteq H$.

(a) Prove that $H$ normalizes $C_G(K)$.

(b) If $H\trianglelefteq G$ and $C_H(K)=\langle1\rangle$, prove that $H$ centralizes $C_G(K)$.
answer: (a) Conjugating $gk=kg$ by $h\in H$ shows $g^h$ centralizes $K^h=K$. (b) In $\bar G=H\,C_G(K)$ both $H$ and $C_G(K)$ are normal with intersection $C_H(K)=1$, so $[H,C_G(K)]=1$.

solutions.title: Disjoint normal subgroups commute
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $g\in C_G(K)$, $h\in H$. For $k\in K$, $k^{h^{-1}}\in K$ since $K\trianglelefteq H$, so $g$ commutes with $k^{h^{-1}}$; conjugating by $h$, $g^h$ commutes with $k$. Thus $g^h\in C_G(K)$ for all $h\in H$, i.e. $H$ normalizes $C_G(K)$.

**(b)** Let $C=C_G(K)$. By (a), $\bar G=HC$ is a subgroup and $C\trianglelefteq\bar G$ (it is normalized by $H$ and by itself). Since $H\trianglelefteq G$, also $H\trianglelefteq\bar G$. Moreover $H\cap C=C_H(K)=1$. For $h\in H$, $c\in C$, the commutator $[h,c]=h^{-1}(c^{-1}hc)\in H$ and $[h,c]=(h^{-1}c^{-1}h)c\in C$, so $[h,c]\in H\cap C=1$. Hence $H$ centralizes $C_G(K)$. ∎

prompt:
In this problem, the word *ideal* always means *two-sided ideal*. Now let $R$ be a (not necessarily commutative) ring with $1$. An ideal $P$ of $R$ is said to be *prime* if, for all ideals $A$ and $B$ of $R$, the inclusion $AB\subseteq P$ implies that $A\subseteq P$ or $B\subseteq P$.

(a) If an ideal $Q$ is not prime, show that there exist ideals $A>Q$ and $B>Q$ with $AB\subseteq Q$.

(b) Let $I$ and $Q$ be ideals of $R$ and assume that $Q$ is maximal with the property that it contains no power of $I$. Show that $Q$ is prime.

(c) Suppose $I$ is a nonnilpotent ideal of $R$. If $R$ satisfies the ascending chain condition on ideals, prove that there exists a prime ideal of $R$ which does not contain $I$.
answer: (a) Replace the witnesses $A',B'$ by $A'+Q$, $B'+Q$. (b) Otherwise $A\supseteq I^m$, $B\supseteq I^k$ with $AB\subseteq Q$ gives $I^{m+k}\subseteq Q$. (c) ACC gives a maximal ideal $Q$ among those containing no power of $I$ (nonempty: $0$); it is prime by (b) and does not contain $I$.

solutions.title: Maximal counterexample
solutions.body:
**(a)** Since $Q$ is not prime, there are ideals $A',B'$ with $A'B'\subseteq Q$, $A'\not\subseteq Q$, $B'\not\subseteq Q$. Let $A=A'+Q$, $B=B'+Q$; these are ideals properly containing $Q$, and $AB\subseteq A'B'+A'Q+QB'+QQ\subseteq Q$.

**(b)** Note $Q\ne R$ (as $R\supseteq I^1$). Suppose $Q$ is not prime and take $A,B\supsetneq Q$ with $AB\subseteq Q$ as in (a). By maximality of $Q$, $A\supseteq I^m$ and $B\supseteq I^k$ for some $m,k\ge1$. Then $I^{m+k}=I^mI^k\subseteq AB\subseteq Q$, contradicting the choice of $Q$. So $Q$ is prime.

**(c)** Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of ideals containing no power of $I$. As $I$ is not nilpotent, $0\in\mathcal S$. ACC on ideals is equivalent to every nonempty family of ideals having a maximal member, so $\mathcal S$ has a maximal member $Q$. By (b), $Q$ is prime, and $I\not\subseteq Q$ since $Q\in\mathcal S$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K\subseteq L$ be a finite degree extension of fields. Suppose that $E$ and $F$ are intermediate fields, each Galois over $K$, and that $L=EF$ is the field generated by $E$ and $F$. (This means that no proper subfield of $L$ contains both $E$ and $F$.)

(a) Prove that $L$ is Galois over $K$.

(b) If $\mathrm{Gal}(E/K)=G$ and $\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)=H$, show that $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $G\times H$.
answer: (a) If $E,F$ split separable $f,g$, then $L$ is generated by the roots of $fg$, so it splits the separable polynomial $\mathrm{lcm}(f,g)$. (b) Restriction $\sigma\mapsto(\sigma|_E,\sigma|_F)$ is an injective homomorphism into $G\times H$.

solutions.title: Splitting fields and restriction
solutions.body:
**(a)** $E$ and $F$ are splitting fields over $K$ of separable polynomials $f,g\in K[x]$. The subfield of $L$ generated over $K$ by the roots of $f$ and $g$ contains $E$ and $F$, hence equals $L$. So $L$ is the splitting field over $K$ of $\mathrm{lcm}(f,g)$, whose irreducible factors each divide $f$ or $g$ and are therefore separable. Hence $L/K$ is normal and separable, i.e. Galois.

**(b)** Let $T=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$. As $E/K$ is normal, every $t\in T$ maps $E$ onto itself, so restriction gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon T\to G$; similarly $\varphi\colon T\to H$. Then $\psi(t)=(\theta(t),\varphi(t))$ is a homomorphism $T\to G\times H$. If $\psi(t)=1$, then $t$ fixes $E$ and $F$ pointwise; the fixed field of $t$ is a subfield of $L$ containing $E$ and $F$, so it is $L$ and $t=1$. Thus $\psi$ is injective and $T\cong\psi(T)\le G\times H$. ∎

prompt:
In this problem, all matrices are viewed over the complex numbers.

(a) For which complex numbers $x$, if any, is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\8&x\end{pmatrix}$ not similar to a diagonal matrix? Explain.

(b) Let $J$ be the $n\times n$ matrix all of whose entries are equal to $1$. Find a diagonal matrix similar to $J$ or prove that none exists.
answer: (a) Exactly $x=9$ and $x=-7$ (the characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-(x+1)\lambda+(x+16)$ has a double root, and the matrix is not scalar). (b) $J\sim\mathrm{diag}(n,0,\dots,0)$.

solutions.title: Characteristic and minimal polynomials
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $A(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\8&x\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is
$$\varphi(\lambda)=\lambda^2-(x+1)\lambda+(x+16).$$
If $\varphi$ has distinct roots, $A(x)$ is diagonalizable. It has a double root iff the discriminant vanishes: $(x+1)^2=4(x+16)$, i.e. $x^2-2x-63=(x-9)(x+7)=0$. For $x=9$, $\varphi=(\lambda-5)^2$; for $x=-7$, $\varphi=(\lambda+3)^2$. If $A(x)$ were then diagonalizable it would be similar to the scalar matrix $\mu I$, hence equal to $\mu I$; but $A(x)$ has off-diagonal entries $-2,8\ne0$. So $A(x)$ is **not** diagonalizable exactly for $x=9$ and $x=-7$.

**(b)** $J^2=nJ$ (each entry of $J^2$ is $n$), so $J$ satisfies $\lambda(\lambda-n)$, which has distinct roots $0,n$ (for $n\ge1$). Hence $J$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues in $\{0,n\}$, say $J\sim D$ with $b$ entries equal to $n$ and the rest $0$. Comparing traces, $n=\mathrm{tr}\,J=bn$, so $b=1$. Thus
$$J\sim D=\mathrm{diag}(n,0,\dots,0).$$
(Equivalently: $\mathrm{rank}\,J=1$, so $D$ has one nonzero entry, which equals $\mathrm{tr}\,J=n$; the vector $(1,\dots,1)$ is an eigenvector for $n$, and the $(n-1)$-dimensional kernel consists of vectors with coordinate sum $0$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $F[x,y]$ be the polynomial ring over the field $F$ in the two indeterminates $x$ and $y$. Suppose $f(x)\in F[x]\subseteq F[x,y]$ and $g(y)\in F[y]\subseteq F[x,y]$ are polynomials of positive degree in the indeterminates $x$ and $y$, respectively. Let $I=(f(x),g(y))$ be the ideal of $F[x,y]$ generated by $f(x)$ and $g(y)$.

(a) Prove that $I\neq F[x,y]$.

(b) If $f(x)=x-\alpha$ and $g(y)=y-\beta$ for some $\alpha,\beta\in F$, show that $I$ is a maximal ideal of $F[x,y]$.
answer: (a) Evaluating at a root $\alpha$ of $f$ and a root $\beta$ of $g$ in $\bar F$ kills $I$ but not $1$. (b) Modulo $I$, $h(x,y)\equiv h(\alpha,\beta)$, so $F[x,y]/I\cong F$, a field.

**(b)** Let $	heta\colon F[x,y]	o F$ be evaluation at $(\alpha, eta)$; it is surjective, so $J=\ker	heta$ is maximal ($F[x,y]/J\cong F$), and $I\subseteq J$. Conversely, $x\equiv\alpha$ and $y\equiv eta\pmod I$, so for any $h$, $h(x,y)\equiv h(\alpha, eta)\pmod I$. If $h\in J$ then $h\equiv0\pmod I$, i.e. $h\in I$. So $I=J$ is maximal. ∎

solutions.title: Dimension count for (a)
solutions.body: For (a) one can also argue: $F[x,y]/(f,g)\cong F[x]/(f)\otimes_FF[y]/(g)$, which has $F$-dimension $\deg f\cdot\deg g>0$; concretely, the monomials $x^iy^j$ with $i<\deg f$, $j<\deg g$ form a basis modulo $I$ (divide by the monic versions of $f$ in $x$ and $g$ in $y$). A nonzero quotient means $I\ne F[x,y]$. For (b), with $\deg f=\deg g=1$ the quotient is $1$-dimensional, spanned by the image of $1$, so $F[x,y]/I\cong F$ is a field and $I$ is maximal. ∎
